topics.title: File Systems versus Database Systems
topics.definition: A file system stores data in separate application files, while a DBMS stores it centrally with controlled sharing and integrity.

children.title: Drawbacks of file processing
children.definition: Data redundancy, inconsistency, difficulty of concurrent access, weak security and program data dependence.

children.title: Advantages of a DBMS
children.definition: Controlled redundancy, shared data, integrity constraints, backup and recovery, security and data independence.

children.title: When a DBMS is not suitable
children.definition: Small single user applications with simple fixed data may not justify the cost and complexity of a DBMS.

card.explanation: In the file processing approach every application owns its own files. The same student address then sits in the library file and again in the accounts file. That copying is redundancy, and when one copy is edited and the other is not, the data becomes inconsistent. Two users editing one file at the same time can overwrite each other, and access is granted for the whole file or not at all. A DBMS keeps the data in one place, lets many programs share it under rules called integrity constraints, and handles backup and recovery. The gain is smaller for a small program used by one person with fixed data, where a DBMS costs more than it returns.
card.example: A college stores fees in one spreadsheet and exam marks in another, and both hold the student phone number. When a student changes the number, only one sheet gets edited, and the office rings the old one.

quiz.q: In file processing, what makes the same address appear differently in two files?
options: Editing one copy and leaving the other alone
The absence of a search key
Two users opening the file at once
quiz.why: Redundancy means several copies exist, and updating only one of them is what produces inconsistency.

quiz.q: Which of these is an advantage a DBMS brings over file processing?
options: Every user keeping a private copy of the data
Faster programs because no software layer sits between
No need for any backup procedure
quiz.why: A DBMS permits redundancy only where it is needed and enforces rules so the copies stay consistent.

quiz.q: A shopkeeper keeps one file of items on a single computer that nothing else reads. What does the card advise?
options: Appoint a database administrator to control access
Add a foreign key to every item
A DBMS may not be worth the cost here
Move to a three schema architecture
quiz.why: Small single user applications with simple fixed data usually cost less to run on plain files.

quiz.q: Which statement about file processing is NOT correct?
options: Security is applied at the whole file level
The same data is often stored in several files
Concurrent access is difficult to control
Files give data independence from the program code
quiz.why: Program data dependence is the drawback: change the file layout and every program reading it must change too.

card.examTip: Write the five drawbacks of file processing in one line each, then the six DBMS advantages opposite them; this comparison is a repeated question.

topics.title: Data Models
topics.definition: A data model is a collection of concepts for describing the structure of a database and the operations allowed on it.

children.title: Hierarchical model
children.definition: Organises data as a tree of parent and child records, where each child has exactly one parent.

children.title: Network model
children.definition: Uses a graph of records where a child may have more than one parent, handled through sets and pointers.

children.title: Relational model
children.definition: Represents data as tables of rows and columns with keys and relationships expressed by matching values.

children.title: Object based and object relational models
children.definition: Store complex objects, classes and inheritance, with object relational systems adding these ideas to relational tables.

children.title: Entity relationship model
children.definition: A conceptual, diagrammatic model of entities, attributes and relationships used before implementation.

card.explanation: A data model is the set of ideas used to describe data before it is stored. The hierarchical model arranges records as a tree where every child has one parent, so one to many data is fast. The network model allows several parents through sets and pointers, but programs must navigate the links step by step. The relational model puts everything in tables whose rows are linked by matching key values, which is why it replaced both. Object based and object relational models add classes and inheritance, and the ER model is the diagram drawn before any of them is implemented.
card.example: A library keeps one member and many books borrowed by that member, which fits the hierarchical model neatly. A university where one student belongs to two departments does not, which is where the network model was used.

quiz.q: Which model organises data as a tree where each child has exactly one parent?
quiz.why: The hierarchical model is a tree of parent and child records with a single parent for each child.

quiz.q: Which model is drawn as a diagram of entities and relationships before implementation?
quiz.why: The ER model is the conceptual, diagrammatic model used at design time, before any table is created.

quiz.q: Why did the relational model replace the hierarchical and network models?
options: It allows a child record to have several parents
Rows are linked by matching key values instead of pointers
It stores data as a single tree
quiz.why: Matching values in columns replace the pointers of the older models, so queries no longer have to follow links.

quiz.q: Which statement about data models is NOT correct?
options: Object relational models add inheritance to tables
The network model uses sets and pointers
The hierarchical model struggles with many to many data
The ER model is implemented directly as the stored records
quiz.why: The ER model is a conceptual design diagram, not a storage structure; it is mapped into tables later.

card.examTip: Draw the three classic models side by side and name one structure each: tree, graph and table. Add the line that the ER model is conceptual.

topics.title: DBMS Architecture
topics.definition: A DBMS is organised in levels so that users, the logical design and the physical storage remain independent of one another.

children.title: Three schema architecture
children.definition: External or view level for individual users, conceptual level for the logical design and internal level for physical storage.

children.title: Data abstraction
children.definition: Hides storage detail from users and shows only the level of detail each user needs.

children.title: Database administrator and users
children.definition: The DBA designs and maintains the schema and controls access, while end users, application programmers and analysts use the data.

children.title: Database languages
children.definition: DDL defines structures, DML manipulates data, DCL controls privileges and TCL manages transactions.

card.explanation: A DBMS is built in three levels so that a change in one place does not spread everywhere. The external or view level is what one user or one application sees. The conceptual level holds the logical design, the tables and the constraints for the whole organisation. The internal level describes how the records are actually laid out on disk. The database administrator, or DBA, owns the schema and the access rights, and four language groups let each role work at its own level.
card.example: A student sees only her own marks in the college portal, while the office sees every student's marks. Both are views over one conceptual table, and neither knows whether the file is hashed or indexed.

quiz.q: Which level of the three schema architecture describes physical storage on disk?
quiz.why: The internal level is the physical schema, describing record layout, indexes and storage structures.

quiz.q: Which language group is used to grant and revoke privileges?
quiz.why: DCL is the data control language used for GRANT and REVOKE; TCL carries COMMIT and ROLLBACK.

quiz.q: Who designs the schema and controls access in an organisation?
quiz.why: The DBA defines the schema, sets the access rights and looks after backup and recovery.

quiz.q: Which statement about DBMS architecture is NOT correct?
options: Data abstraction hides storage detail from the user
The external level holds individual user views
DDL is used to define the schema
Every user sees the whole conceptual schema
quiz.why: Abstraction means each user sees only their own view, never the entire conceptual schema.

card.examTip: Sketch the three boxes external, conceptual and internal with the two mappings between them, and write one line on each level.

topics.title: Data Independence
topics.definition: Data independence means that a change at one level of the schema does not force changes at a higher level.

children.title: Logical data independence
children.definition: Changing the conceptual schema, such as adding a column, need not change the external views or the application programs.

children.title: Physical data independence
children.definition: Changing storage structures such as adding an index need not change the conceptual schema.

children.title: How independence is achieved
children.definition: By keeping separate schema levels and mapping each level to the next.

card.explanation: Data independence is the reason a database can be changed without rewriting every program. Logical independence means the conceptual schema can change, for example by adding a column, while the existing views keep working. Physical independence means the storage can change, for example by adding an index, without touching the conceptual schema. Both work because each level is defined separately and a mapping connects it to the next. Physical independence is the easier of the two, because storage details are already hidden from the design.
card.example: The college adds an Aadhaar column to the student table. The existing report programs keep running, because their views still ask only for the old columns.

quiz.q: Adding a new column to the conceptual schema without changing existing applications is an example of:
quiz.why: Logical independence protects external views and programs when the conceptual schema changes.

quiz.q: Adding an index to speed up searches without altering the table design is an example of:
options: No independence, because the schema changed
quiz.why: Physical independence means changes at the internal level do not reach the conceptual schema.

quiz.q: How is data independence actually achieved?
options: By storing every table in one file
By giving every user a private copy of the data
By keeping separate schema levels and mapping each to the next
By rewriting the applications after every change
quiz.why: The mappings between the external, conceptual and internal levels are what absorb the change.

quiz.q: Which statement about data independence is NOT correct?
options: A view can hide a newly added column from an old program
Physical independence means storage changes do not reach the conceptual schema
Separate schema levels with mappings make independence possible
Logical independence means the internal file layout can change freely
quiz.why: Changing the internal file layout is physical independence; logical independence is about the conceptual schema.

card.examTip: Write two definitions, one for each kind, with one example each: adding a column is logical, adding an index is physical.

topics.title: Data Modelling Using the Entity Relationship Model
topics.definition: The ER model describes data as entities, their attributes and the relationships between them, drawn as a diagram.

children.title: Entity and entity set
children.definition: An entity is a real world object such as a student and an entity set is a collection of similar entities.

children.title: Attributes and their types
children.definition: Simple, composite, single valued, multivalued, derived and key attributes describe the properties of an entity.

children.title: Relationship and relationship set
children.definition: An association among entities such as enrols between student and course.

children.title: Degree and cardinality ratio
children.definition: Degree counts participating entity sets; cardinality is one to one, one to many, many to one or many to many.

children.title: Participation constraints
children.definition: Total participation means every entity takes part, partial means only some do.

children.title: Keys in ER design
children.definition: Super key, candidate key, primary key and foreign key identify entities and link them.

children.title: Weak entity set
children.definition: An entity set without a key of its own, identified only through its owner entity with a partial key.

children.title: ER diagram notation
children.definition: Rectangles for entities, ellipses for attributes, diamonds for relationships, double lines for total participation.

card.explanation: The ER model is drawn before any table exists. An entity is a real object such as one student, and an entity set is the collection of all students. Attributes describe an entity and may be simple, composite, single valued, multivalued, derived or a key. A relationship such as enrols links two entity sets. Cardinality says whether it is one to one, one to many, many to one or many to many. Participation says whether every entity must take part. An entity set with no key of its own is a weak entity set, identified through its owner and a partial key.
card.example: In a college, Student and Course are entity sets and Enrols is a many to many relationship between them. A fee receipt means nothing without the student it belongs to, so it is a weak entity set.

quiz.q: In an ER diagram, which shape is used to show a relationship?
quiz.why: Rectangles are entities, ellipses are attributes, diamonds are relationships and double lines show total participation.

quiz.q: A fee receipt cannot be identified without the student it belongs to. What is it called?
quiz.why: A weak entity set has no key of its own and is identified through its owner plus a partial key.

quiz.q: Which attribute type is calculated from another attribute rather than stored?
quiz.why: Age worked out from a date of birth is the usual example; it is computed, not kept on disk.

quiz.q: Which statement about ER modelling is NOT correct?
options: A foreign key links one entity set to another
Cardinality may be one to one, one to many, many to one or many to many
Total participation means every entity of the set takes part
Degree is the number of attributes an entity has
quiz.why: Degree counts the entity sets taking part in a relationship, not the attributes of an entity.

card.examTip: Practise the notation: rectangle, ellipse, diamond, double rectangle, double ellipse, double line. Most questions ask for a full ER diagram.

topics.title: Enhanced ER Modelling
topics.definition: Enhanced ER modelling adds abstraction tools such as specialisation, generalisation, aggregation and categories.

children.title: Specialisation and generalisation
children.definition: Specialisation splits a superclass into subclasses, generalisation combines similar entities into a superclass.

children.title: Attribute inheritance
children.definition: A subclass inherits all attributes of its superclass and adds its own.

children.title: Constraints on specialisation
children.definition: Disjoint or overlapping subclasses, and total or partial participation in the specialisation.

children.title: Aggregation
children.definition: Treats a relationship as a higher level entity so it can take part in another relationship.

children.title: Category and union type
children.definition: A subclass whose members come from a union of several different superclasses, shown with a union circle.

card.explanation: Enhanced ER adds ideas from object oriented thinking to the plain ER diagram. Specialisation splits a superclass into subclasses, while generalisation does the reverse and combines similar entities. A subclass inherits every attribute of its superclass and adds its own. The splitting can be constrained as disjoint or overlapping, and as total or partial. Aggregation treats a whole relationship as one higher level entity so it can join another relationship. A category collects its members from several different superclasses.
card.example: In a college, Person generalises Student and Teacher, and Student specialises into Undergraduate and Postgraduate. A student who also works as a lab assistant belongs to two subclasses at once, which makes the specialisation overlapping.

quiz.q: Combining several similar entity sets into one higher level entity set is called:
quiz.why: Generalisation works bottom up, while specialisation works top down from a superclass to its subclasses.

quiz.q: What does a subclass receive from its superclass?
options: Only the relationships, never the attributes
All of its attributes, through attribute inheritance
quiz.why: Attribute inheritance gives the subclass every superclass attribute plus whatever it adds itself.

quiz.q: Treating a relationship as a higher level entity so it can take part in another relationship is called:
quiz.why: Aggregation lets a relationship such as Enrols become an entity that can join another relationship.

quiz.q: Which statement about enhanced ER is NOT correct?
options: Generalisation moves from several entity sets to one superclass
A subclass may be constrained as disjoint or overlapping
A category is a union type drawn with a circle marked U
Specialisation requires every superclass entity to sit in some subclass
quiz.why: Requiring every entity to belong is the total constraint, which is optional; partial specialisation allows an entity in no subclass.

card.examTip: Draw the superclass with the ISA triangle, mark disjoint or overlapping, mark total or partial, then add one example.

modules.title: Relational Model, SQL, Design and Normalisation

topics.title: Relational Model Concepts
topics.definition: The relational model stores data in relations (tables) of tuples (rows) and attributes (columns) drawn from domains.

children.title: Relation, tuple, attribute and domain
children.definition: A relation is a table, a tuple is a row, an attribute is a named column and a domain is the set of allowed values.

children.title: Degree and cardinality
children.definition: Degree counts the attributes or columns and cardinality counts the tuples or rows.

children.title: Keys of a relation
children.definition: Super key uniquely identifies a tuple, candidate keys are minimal super keys, one becomes the primary key and foreign keys reference other relations.

children.title: Integrity constraints
children.definition: Entity integrity forbids NULL primary keys and referential integrity requires a foreign key to match some existing primary key or be NULL.

children.title: Codd rules
children.definition: Twelve rules described by E F Codd that a full relational DBMS should satisfy.

card.explanation: The relational model keeps everything in one structure, the relation, which looks like a table. A tuple is one row, an attribute is one named column and a domain is the set of values that column may hold. Degree counts the attributes and cardinality counts the tuples. Keys identify rows: a super key is any unique set of attributes, and a candidate key is a minimal super key. One candidate key is chosen as the primary key, and a foreign key points at a primary key in another relation. Two rules guard the data: entity integrity forbids a null primary key, and referential integrity forbids a foreign key with no matching primary key.
card.example: A Student table with four columns has degree 4, and with 900 rows it has cardinality 900. RollNo is the primary key, and DeptID in the same table is a foreign key pointing at Department.

quiz.q: What is the term for one row of a relation?
quiz.why: A tuple is a row, an attribute is a column and a domain is the set of allowed values.

quiz.q: A relation has 6 columns and 240 rows. What are its degree and cardinality?
quiz.why: Degree counts the attributes or columns, and cardinality counts the tuples or rows.

quiz.q: Which rule is broken when a row holds a foreign key value that no primary key contains?
quiz.why: Referential integrity requires every non null foreign key to match a primary key that exists.

quiz.q: Which statement about keys is NOT correct?
options: One candidate key is chosen as the primary key
A candidate key is a minimal super key
A relation may have more than one candidate key
A foreign key must be unique within its own table
quiz.why: A foreign key is often repeated, because many rows may point at the same parent row.

quiz.q: How many rules did E F Codd describe for a full relational DBMS?
quiz.why: Codd gave twelve rules, sometimes numbered from zero, that a relational system should satisfy.

card.examTip: Start with relation, tuple, attribute and domain, then give degree and cardinality, then the two integrity rules. Marks are usually split this way.

topics.title: Relational Algebra
topics.definition: Relational algebra is a procedural query language of operators that take relations and produce a new relation.

children.title: Selection and projection
children.definition: Selection (sigma) chooses rows satisfying a condition; projection (pi) chooses a subset of columns.

children.title: Set operations
children.definition: Union, intersection, set difference and Cartesian product combine relations with compatible schemas.

children.title: Join operations
children.definition: Theta join, equi join and natural join combine matching rows; outer joins keep unmatched rows padded with NULL.

children.title: Division operation
children.definition: Returns tuples of one relation that match every tuple of another, used for questions like "students who took all courses".

children.title: Renaming and assignment
children.definition: The rho operator renames relations or attributes and the assignment operator names intermediate results.

card.explanation: Relational algebra is procedural, which means a query says which operators to apply and in what order. Selection, written sigma, keeps the rows that satisfy a condition, and projection, written pi, keeps only the columns named. Union, intersection, set difference and Cartesian product combine two relations whose schemas match. A join puts matching rows from two relations together. A theta join allows any comparison, an equi join uses equality, and a natural join drops the duplicate column. Outer joins keep unmatched rows and pad the missing side with null. Division answers the all questions, such as students who took every course, and the rho operator renames relations or attributes.
card.example: To list the names of students in the CSE department, first select the rows where Dept equals CSE, then project the Name column. To find students who took every course, divide the enrolment table by the course table.

quiz.q: Which operator keeps only the rows that satisfy a condition?
quiz.why: Selection, written sigma, filters rows, while projection, written pi, picks columns.

quiz.q: Which operator answers the question students who enrolled in every course?
quiz.why: Division returns the tuples that match every tuple of a second relation.

quiz.q: What does a natural join do that an equi join does not?
options: It keeps unmatched rows padded with null
It requires the two schemas to be identical
It allows comparisons other than equality
It removes the duplicate join column
quiz.why: Both match on equality, but the natural join shows the shared column only once.

quiz.q: Which statement about relational algebra is NOT correct?
options: Projection always increases the number of rows
An outer join keeps unmatched rows with null padding
Every operator takes relations and returns a relation
Set operations need the two relations to be union compatible
quiz.why: Projection can reduce the row count, because duplicate rows are removed once columns are dropped.

quiz.q: Which operator gives a name to a relation or to one of its attributes?
quiz.why: Rho is the rename operator; sigma selects and pi projects.

card.examTip: Write the symbol for each operator first, then one line on what it returns. Questions usually ask for an expression, so keep the order of operations visible.

topics.title: SQL: Basic and Complex Queries
topics.definition: SQL is the standard language for defining and querying relational databases, written as declarative statements.

children.title: DDL, DML, DCL and TCL
children.definition: DDL creates and alters structures, DML selects and modifies rows, DCL grants privileges and TCL commits or rolls back transactions.

children.title: Basic SELECT queries
children.definition: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition with DISTINCT, ORDER BY, BETWEEN, IN and LIKE.

children.title: Aggregate functions and grouping
children.definition: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX with GROUP BY and HAVING for conditions on groups.

children.title: Joins in SQL
children.definition: Inner join, left, right and full outer joins in both the classic and ANSI syntax.

children.title: Subqueries and correlated queries
children.definition: Nested SELECT statements, including EXISTS, ANY and ALL comparisons against inner results.

children.title: UPDATE, DELETE and INSERT
children.definition: Statements that modify the contents of existing relations.

children.title: Views
children.definition: A stored query acting as a virtual table, used for security and simplified access; updatable only under restrictions.

children.title: Constraints
children.definition: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK and DEFAULT enforce rules at the schema level.

card.explanation: SQL is declarative, so a query describes the result wanted and the system decides how to fetch it. The language has four parts: DDL defines structures, DML reads and changes rows, DCL grants privileges and TCL commits or rolls back work. A basic query names the columns to return, the table to read and a WHERE condition. DISTINCT, ORDER BY, BETWEEN, IN and LIKE shape the result. Aggregates such as COUNT and SUM work on groups made by GROUP BY, and HAVING filters the groups themselves. Joins bring rows from two tables together, and a subquery is a SELECT inside another SELECT. A view stores the query itself and acts as a virtual table for the user.
card.example: To find departments with more than 60 students, group by DeptID and count the rows. Put the condition on the count in HAVING, not in WHERE.

quiz.q: Which clause filters the groups produced by GROUP BY?
quiz.why: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, and HAVING filters the groups after counting.

quiz.q: GRANT and REVOKE belong to which part of SQL?
quiz.why: DCL is the data control language; TCL holds COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT.

quiz.q: Which statement about SQL is NOT correct?
options: A subquery may appear only in the SELECT clause
A view stores the query, not a separate copy of the rows
HAVING is applied after GROUP BY
WHERE is applied before any grouping takes place
quiz.why: A subquery can appear in SELECT, FROM, WHERE and HAVING clauses, and with EXISTS, ANY and ALL.

quiz.q: A report must list every department and show null where a department has no students. Which join is needed?
quiz.why: A left outer join keeps every row of the left table and pads the missing right side with null.

quiz.q: Which keyword removes duplicate rows from a result?
quiz.why: DISTINCT removes repeated rows from the result; UNIQUE is a constraint written on a column.

card.examTip: For a query question, write the SELECT and FROM line first, then WHERE, then GROUP BY and HAVING, then ORDER BY. Note that HAVING needs GROUP BY.

topics.title: Relational Calculus
topics.definition: Relational calculus is a non procedural query language that describes what result is wanted rather than how to compute it.

children.title: Tuple relational calculus
children.definition: Describes the set of tuples t for which a predicate is true, written as {t | P(t)}.

children.title: Domain relational calculus
children.definition: Describes the result by listing the domains of its attributes with conditions on them.

children.title: Expressiveness and safety
children.definition: Both calculi are equivalent in power to relational algebra; safe expressions avoid infinite results.

card.explanation: Relational calculus is non procedural, so a query states the condition the answer must satisfy instead of listing operators. Tuple relational calculus asks for the set of tuples t for which a predicate is true, written as t such that P of t. Domain relational calculus does the same by naming the domain variables for the columns and putting conditions on them. Both are equal in expressive power to relational algebra, so anything written in one can be written in the other. Safe expressions are required, because an unsafe one can produce an infinite set of tuples.
card.example: Ask for every student whose department is CSE, rather than saying filter the file and then pick the name column. The system chooses the operators itself.

quiz.q: What kind of language is relational calculus?
quiz.why: It says what is wanted; relational algebra says which operators to apply and in what order.

quiz.q: Tuple relational calculus is written in which form?
options: t such that P of t
quiz.why: The result is the set of tuples t for which the predicate P is true.

quiz.q: Which statement about the two calculi is NOT correct?
options: An unsafe expression can return an infinite set of tuples
A calculus query must list the operators used to reach the answer
Tuple calculus and domain calculus have the same expressive power
Both are equivalent in power to relational algebra
quiz.why: Listing the operators is what relational algebra does; calculus states only the condition.

quiz.q: Why is the safety condition imposed on calculus expressions?
options: To force the use of an index
To make the query run faster
To stop the result from being an infinite set
To allow null values in the answer
quiz.why: A safe expression can only draw values from the database or from the constants written in it.

card.examTip: Contrast the two in one table: algebra is procedural with operators, calculus is declarative with predicates. Add that both have equal expressive power.

topics.title: Overview of Commercial RDBMSs
topics.definition: Commercial systems such as Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL and DB2 implement SQL with vendor extensions.

children.title: Features to compare
children.definition: Storage limits, concurrency control, recovery, partitioning, security, replication and cost.

children.title: Oracle and SQL Server
children.definition: Enterprise systems with PL/SQL and T-SQL procedural extensions and rich administration tools.

children.title: MySQL and PostgreSQL
children.definition: Widely used open source systems, one favoured for web applications and the other for standards compliance.

card.explanation: Every commercial system implements standard SQL and then adds its own extensions on top. Oracle and SQL Server are enterprise products with the PL/SQL and T-SQL procedural languages and a wide set of administration tools. MySQL and PostgreSQL are open source; MySQL is common behind web applications and PostgreSQL is known for following the standards closely. Choosing between them means comparing storage limits, concurrency control, recovery, partitioning, security, replication and licence cost. DB2 is IBM's system and is found mostly in large established installations.
card.example: A startup building a web application with no licence budget usually starts on MySQL or PostgreSQL. A bank replacing a mainframe system pays for Oracle or DB2 and expects the administration tools that come with it.

quiz.q: Which procedural language belongs to Oracle?
quiz.why: Oracle uses PL/SQL, while SQL Server uses T-SQL.

quiz.q: Which two of these systems are open source?
quiz.why: MySQL and PostgreSQL are the widely used open source systems; the others carry licence costs.

quiz.q: Which statement about choosing an RDBMS is NOT correct?
options: Recovery and concurrency control affect the choice
Every system behaves identically because all of them implement SQL
Licence cost is one of the features compared
Replication and partitioning affect the choice
quiz.why: Vendor extensions, storage limits and administration tools differ, so the systems are not interchangeable in practice.

quiz.q: A team needs a standards compliant open source database for a college project with no budget. Which fits best?
quiz.why: PostgreSQL is open source and is known for following the standards closely.

card.examTip: Answer comparison questions with a table: system, vendor, licence, procedural language and one typical use.

topics.title: Database Design and Functional Dependencies
topics.definition: Good relational design starts from dependencies among attributes that reveal redundancy and update anomalies.

children.title: Informal design guidelines
children.definition: Keep semantics clear, reduce redundancy and avoid NULL heavy relations.

children.title: Functional dependency
children.definition: X determines Y means any two tuples agreeing on X must also agree on Y, written X -> Y.

children.title: Partial and transitive dependency
children.definition: A partial dependency uses only part of a composite key; a transitive dependency reaches a non-key attribute through another non-key attribute.

children.title: Armstrong axioms
children.definition: Reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity generate all dependencies, with union, decomposition and pseudotransitivity as derived rules.

children.title: Closure and candidate key computation
children.definition: The closure of an attribute set gives everything it determines, and a minimal attribute set whose closure is the whole relation is a candidate key.

children.title: Canonical cover
children.definition: A minimal equivalent set of functional dependencies with no redundant dependencies or attributes.

children.title: Decomposition and its properties
children.definition: Splitting a relation into smaller relations, checked for lossless join and dependency preservation.

card.explanation: A functional dependency says that if two rows agree on X, they must also agree on Y, written X arrow Y. Finding the dependencies in a table shows where the same fact is stored more than once. A partial dependency uses only part of a composite key, and a transitive dependency reaches a non key attribute through another non key attribute. Armstrong's axioms of reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity generate every dependency that follows from a given set. The closure of an attribute set is everything it determines, and a minimal set whose closure covers the whole relation is a candidate key. Splitting a table is called decomposition, and a good one keeps the join lossless and the dependencies preserved.
card.example: In a table holding RollNo, StudentName and DeptHead, RollNo determines StudentName and DeptHead. RollNo also determines Dept, and Dept determines DeptHead, so DeptHead is transitively dependent on the key.

quiz.q: What does the functional dependency X arrow Y mean?
options: X and Y together form the primary key
X and Y must always hold the same value
Any two rows agreeing on X must also agree on Y
quiz.why: The left side fixes the right side, so two rows with the same X cannot carry different Y values.

quiz.q: Which of these is a derived rule rather than one of Armstrong's basic axioms?
quiz.why: Union, decomposition and pseudotransitivity are proved from the three basic axioms.

quiz.q: Which statement about dependencies is NOT correct?
options: The closure of a set is everything that set determines
A candidate key must contain every attribute of the relation
A partial dependency depends on part of a composite key
A transitive dependency passes through a non key attribute
quiz.why: A candidate key is a minimal attribute set whose closure covers the whole relation, not the relation itself.

quiz.q: A table is split into two. Which property says that joining them back returns exactly the original rows?
quiz.why: A lossless decomposition guarantees that no spurious rows appear when the tables are joined again.

quiz.q: What is a canonical cover?
options: The set of all candidate keys
A decomposition with no transitive dependency
A cover containing every possible dependency
A minimal equivalent set of dependencies with nothing redundant
quiz.why: Extraneous attributes and redundant dependencies are removed, but the closure stays the same.

card.examTip: List the dependencies, compute each closure, mark the candidate key, then name the dependency that breaks 2NF or 3NF.

topics.title: Normal Forms
topics.definition: Normalisation removes redundancy and anomalies by checking a relation against progressively stricter normal forms.

children.title: Why normalisation is needed
children.definition: Unnormalised relations suffer update, insertion and deletion anomalies along with wasted space.

children.title: 1NF (First Normal Form)
children.definition: All attributes hold atomic single values - no multivalued attributes or repeating groups.

children.title: 2NF (Second Normal Form)
children.definition: In 1NF and no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on part of a candidate key.

children.title: 3NF (Third Normal Form)
children.definition: In 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key.

children.title: BCNF (Boyce Codd Normal Form)
children.definition: For every non trivial dependency X -> Y, X must be a super key - stricter than 3NF.

children.title: 4NF (Fourth Normal Form)
children.definition: In BCNF and free of multivalued dependencies, which occur when independent multivalued facts are stored together.

children.title: 5NF (Fifth Normal Form)
children.definition: Also called project join normal form, where a relation cannot be decomposed any further without loss.

children.title: Denormalisation
children.definition: Deliberately relaxing normal forms to reduce joins and improve read performance in reporting systems.

card.explanation: A table that is not normalised repeats the same fact in many rows, which causes insertion, update and deletion anomalies. First normal form requires every attribute to hold one atomic value, so no repeating groups or multivalued cells. Second normal form removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key, and third normal form removes transitive dependencies on the key. BCNF is stricter: for every non trivial dependency, the left side must be a super key. Fourth normal form removes multivalued dependencies, fifth normal form removes join dependencies, and denormalisation deliberately steps back to make reporting faster.
card.example: A row storing CSE and IT together in one Department column is not in first normal form. Splitting it into two rows fixes the cell and makes counting departments possible.

quiz.q: Which normal form requires every attribute to hold a single atomic value?
quiz.why: First normal form removes repeating groups and multivalued attributes.

quiz.q: A relation is in 1NF and has no partial dependency on part of a candidate key. Which form is it in?
quiz.why: Removing partial dependencies on a composite key is exactly the step from 1NF to 2NF.

quiz.q: How does BCNF differ from 3NF?
options: BCNF is a weaker form than 3NF
BCNF allows transitive dependencies that 3NF forbids
BCNF requires the left side of every dependency to be a super key
BCNF applies only to single attribute keys
quiz.why: That single condition makes BCNF stricter, and some relations in 3NF still fail it.

quiz.q: Which statement about normalisation is NOT correct?
options: Denormalisation is sometimes chosen to speed up reporting
Higher normal forms reduce redundancy and anomalies
A relation in 4NF is free of multivalued dependencies
A relation in 3NF is always in BCNF as well
quiz.why: BCNF is stricter than 3NF, so there are relations in 3NF that still violate BCNF.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three classic update anomalies?
quiz.why: Insertion, deletion and update anomalies come from redundancy; concurrency is handled by transaction control.

card.examTip: Give one line per form: 1NF atomic, 2NF no partial, 3NF no transitive, BCNF super key.

topics.title: Query Processing and Cost Estimation
topics.definition: Query processing turns an SQL statement into an executable plan whose cost is estimated to pick the cheapest strategy.

children.title: Parsing, validation and translation
children.definition: The query is checked for syntax and semantics and converted into a relational algebra expression.

children.title: Optimisation and plan generation
children.definition: Equivalent expressions and access paths are compared to choose an efficient execution plan.

children.title: Algorithms for executing query operations
children.definition: Full table scan or index scan for selection, nested loop, sort merge and hash join for joins, external sorting for large data.

children.title: Cost estimation
children.definition: Estimates block transfers and disk seeks using statistics such as number of tuples, block factor and selectivity.

children.title: Heuristic optimisation rules
children.definition: Push selections down, then projections, and perform the most restrictive operations first.

card.explanation: A query passes through several steps before a single row is read. The parser checks the syntax and the validator checks that the tables and columns exist. The translator then turns the statement into a relational algebra expression. The optimiser compares equivalent expressions and access paths and picks the cheapest plan it can find. Cost is estimated mainly in block transfers and disk seeks. The estimate uses statistics such as the number of tuples, the blocking factor and the selectivity of a condition. Simple heuristics help too: push selections down before joins, and do the most restrictive operation first.
card.example: A selection that keeps 5 rows out of 100,000 should run before the join, not after it. Pushing it down means the join works on 5 rows instead of 100,000.

quiz.q: Which step checks that the tables and columns named in a query really exist?
quiz.why: Validation checks the query against the catalogue, after the syntax has been accepted.

quiz.q: What is query cost usually measured in?
options: Lines of SQL and number of joins
quiz.why: Disk access dominates query time, so the estimate counts blocks moved and seeks performed.

quiz.q: Which heuristic rule helps most when optimising by hand?
options: Sort every table before reading it
Perform selections and projections as early as possible
quiz.why: Pushing selections and projections down shrinks the data before the expensive join runs.

quiz.q: Which statement about query processing is NOT correct?
options: The optimiser always finds the cheapest possible plan
The translator produces a relational algebra expression
The optimiser compares several equivalent plans
Selectivity helps estimate how many rows a condition returns
quiz.why: Optimisers search a limited space of plans, so they aim for a good plan rather than a guaranteed best one.

card.examTip: Draw the pipeline as parse, validate, translate, optimise, execute, and add the note that cost means block transfers plus seeks.

topics.title: Transaction Processing and Properties
topics.definition: A transaction is a logical unit of work that must either complete fully or leave the database unchanged.

children.title: Transaction operations
children.definition: read_item, write_item, commit and rollback are the basic operations of a transaction.

children.title: ACID properties
children.definition: Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability describe the guarantees a DBMS must provide.

children.title: Transaction states
children.definition: Active, partially committed, committed, failed and aborted states trace the life of a transaction.

children.title: Desirable additional properties
children.definition: Fine granularity of data items and protection from crashes and concurrent interference.

card.explanation: A transaction is one logical unit of work, such as transferring money between two accounts. Its basic operations are read item and write item, and it ends with commit or rollback. Four properties are required: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, remembered as ACID. Atomicity means all or nothing, and consistency means the database still obeys its rules at the end. Isolation means a transaction never sees another's partial work, and durability means committed work survives a crash. A transaction moves through the states active, partially committed, committed, failed and aborted.
card.example: Transferring 500 rupees between two accounts needs a debit and a credit. If the power fails after the debit, atomicity rolls the half done work back so the money is not lost.

quiz.q: Which ACID property says that a transaction is all or nothing?
quiz.why: Atomicity means every operation of the transaction happens, or none of them does.

quiz.q: Which ACID property guarantees that committed work survives a crash?
quiz.why: Durability is what keeps a committed transaction on stable storage after a failure.

quiz.q: A transaction has written its last statement but the system has not confirmed it yet. Which state is it in?
quiz.why: The partially committed state sits between the final write and the commit record.

quiz.q: Which statement about transactions is NOT correct?
options: Isolation lets a transaction read another's uncommitted changes
A transaction moves the database from one consistent state to another
Read item and write item are the basic operations
Rollback undoes the work of the current transaction
quiz.why: Isolation hides uncommitted work from other transactions; reading it is the dirty read problem.

quiz.q: Which pair of operations marks the two ways a transaction can end?
quiz.why: Commit makes the changes permanent and rollback undoes them; the others are internal steps.

card.examTip: Expand ACID one word at a time with a line each, then draw the five states with arrows into committed and aborted.

topics.title: Serializability
topics.definition: A schedule is serializable when its effect equals that of some serial order of the same transactions.

children.title: Schedules and their types
children.definition: Serial schedules run transactions one after another; non-serial schedules interleave them.

children.title: Conflict serializability
children.definition: Two different transactions accessing the same item with at least one write conflict; the precedence graph must be acyclic.

children.title: View serializability
children.definition: A weaker condition requiring the same reads-from relations and the same final writes.

children.title: Recoverable and cascade-less schedules
children.definition: A schedule is recoverable if a transaction commits only after all transactions it read from have committed; cascading rollback is avoided by strict schedules.

card.explanation: A schedule is the order in which the operations of several transactions actually run. A serial schedule runs one transaction to the end before starting the next, which is correct but slow, so systems interleave them instead. An interleaved schedule is conflict serializable when it can be swapped into some serial order by exchanging non conflicting operations. The test is the precedence graph: if it has no cycle, the schedule is conflict serializable. View serializability is a weaker test that compares who read what and who wrote the final value. A schedule is recoverable if a transaction commits only after every transaction it read from has committed.
card.example: T1 reads an account and T2 writes it, so T1 must come before T2 in the precedence graph. If T2 also reads something T1 writes, the graph has a cycle and the schedule is not serializable.

quiz.q: What is a schedule called when transactions run one after another with no interleaving?
quiz.why: A serial schedule runs each transaction to completion before the next begins, so it is always correct.

quiz.q: How is conflict serializability tested?
options: By comparing the final values only
By locking every item until commit
By counting the reads and writes in the schedule
By checking the precedence graph for a cycle
quiz.why: An acyclic precedence graph means the operations can be reordered into some serial schedule.

quiz.q: Which statement about serializability is NOT correct?
options: A serial schedule interleaves operations from several transactions
Every conflict serializable schedule is also view serializable
View serializability is the weaker of the two conditions
A cyclic precedence graph rules out conflict serializability
quiz.why: Interleaving is what a non serial schedule does; a serial schedule keeps the transactions apart.

quiz.q: T1 reads a value written by T2 and commits before T2 commits. Which property is missing?
quiz.why: A recoverable schedule makes a transaction wait to commit until everything it read from has committed.

quiz.q: Which schedule avoids cascading rollback by forbidding reads of uncommitted writes?
quiz.why: A cascadeless schedule allows a read only after the transaction that wrote the value has committed.

card.examTip: Draw the precedence graph for the given schedule, list the edges, then state the verdict from the cycle.

topics.title: Transaction Support in SQL
topics.definition: SQL supports explicit transaction control with COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT statements and isolation levels.

children.title: COMMIT and ROLLBACK
children.definition: COMMIT makes changes permanent while ROLLBACK undoes changes of the current transaction.

children.title: SAVEPOINT and partial rollback
children.definition: Marks an intermediate point to which the transaction can roll back without losing earlier work.

children.title: Isolation levels
children.definition: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE trade correctness against concurrency.

children.title: Concurrency problems controlled by levels
children.definition: Dirty read, non repeatable read and phantom read.

card.explanation: SQL lets a programmer control a transaction directly instead of leaving it to the system. COMMIT makes the changes permanent and ROLLBACK undoes them, taking the database back to where the transaction began. SAVEPOINT marks a point inside the transaction, so a rollback can return there and keep the earlier work. Four isolation levels trade correctness for concurrency: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read and serializable. The lower levels allow dirty reads, non repeatable reads and phantom rows, which the higher levels prevent at the cost of waiting.
card.example: A batch job inserts 500 rows and fails at row 480. A savepoint placed every 100 rows lets the job roll back to row 400 and carry on instead of losing everything.

quiz.q: Which statement undoes the work of the current transaction?
quiz.why: ROLLBACK returns the database to the state before the transaction began; COMMIT makes the work permanent.

quiz.q: What is a SAVEPOINT used for?
options: To mark a point that a rollback can return to
To lock a table until commit
To commit part of the transaction permanently
quiz.why: A rollback to a savepoint keeps the work done before the mark and discards only what came after it.

quiz.q: Which isolation level is the strictest?
quiz.why: Serializable gives the effect of running transactions one at a time, which costs the most concurrency.

quiz.q: A transaction reads a row, and a second read in the same transaction returns a different value. What is this called?
quiz.why: A non repeatable read happens when another transaction commits an update between the two reads.

quiz.q: Which statement about isolation levels is NOT correct?
options: Higher levels reduce the amount of concurrency
Read uncommitted allows a dirty read
Repeatable read stops a value changing between two reads
Serializable permits phantom rows to appear
quiz.why: Serializable is the level that prevents phantom rows; the lower levels are the ones that allow them.

card.examTip: List the four levels in order and name the problem each one removes: dirty read, non repeatable read, phantom read.

topics.title: Locking Techniques
topics.definition: Locking prevents conflicting accesses by making a transaction acquire a lock before reading or writing an item.

children.title: Shared and exclusive locks
children.definition: A shared lock allows reading by many transactions while an exclusive lock allows one writer and blocks everyone else.

children.title: Binary locking versus shared exclusive locking
children.definition: Binary locks are locked or unlocked; shared exclusive locks distinguish readers from writers.

children.title: Two phase locking (2PL)
children.definition: A growing phase acquires locks and a shrinking phase releases them, which guarantees conflict serializability.

children.title: Strict and rigorous 2PL
children.definition: Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit, and rigorous 2PL holds all locks until commit, both easing recovery.

children.title: Deadlock and starvation
children.definition: Deadlock is a circular wait for locks and starvation is a transaction repeatedly losing the competition; both must be handled.

children.title: Lock conversion
children.definition: Upgrading a shared lock to exclusive or downgrading it the other way, which must respect the two phases.

card.explanation: Locking makes a transaction ask permission before it touches a data item. A shared lock allows many readers at once, while an exclusive lock gives one writer the item and blocks everyone else. Two phase locking is the rule that guarantees conflict serializability. It has a growing phase that takes locks and a shrinking phase that releases them, and no lock is taken after the first release. Strict two phase locking holds exclusive locks until commit, which keeps recovery simple. Two problems remain: deadlock, where transactions wait for each other in a circle, and starvation, where one transaction keeps losing the competition.
card.example: Two clerks edit the same row at once, and the first takes an exclusive lock so the second waits. If each then waits for the item the other holds, the system must abort one of them.

quiz.q: Which lock allows many transactions to read the same item at once?
quiz.why: A shared lock is for reading, so several transactions may hold it together; an exclusive lock is for one writer.

quiz.q: What does two phase locking guarantee?
quiz.why: Growing then shrinking, with no new lock after the first release, gives a serializable order.

quiz.q: Which statement about two phase locking is NOT correct?
options: The shrinking phase only releases locks
Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit
Two phase locking can never produce a deadlock
The growing phase only acquires locks
quiz.why: Two phase locking guarantees serializability, not deadlock freedom; waiting for locks can still form a cycle.

quiz.q: T1 holds a lock on A and wants B, while T2 holds B and wants A. What has happened?
quiz.why: A circular wait for locks is a deadlock, and one of the transactions must be rolled back.

quiz.q: Upgrading a shared lock to an exclusive one is called:
quiz.why: Conversion changes the mode of a lock, and it may only happen during the growing phase.

card.examTip: State the two phase rule, then draw a transaction with an up arrow for growing and a down arrow for shrinking, marking the lock point.

topics.title: Timestamp Ordering and Validation Techniques
topics.definition: Timestamp ordering orders transactions by their start time, and validation methods check for conflicts only at commit time.

children.title: Timestamp ordering protocol
children.definition: Each item keeps the read and write timestamps of the last transaction that accessed it, and conflicting older operations are rejected and restarted.

children.title: Thomas write rule
children.definition: Ignores an obsolete write that a later transaction has already overwritten.

children.title: Optimistic (validation based) concurrency control
children.definition: Transactions run freely and are validated in three phases: read, validation and write.

children.title: Comparison with locking
children.definition: Timestamp and validation methods avoid deadlock because they never make a transaction wait for a lock.

card.explanation: Timestamp ordering gives every transaction a start time and forces conflicting operations to obey that order. Each item remembers who last read and wrote it, and an operation that arrives too late is refused and its transaction restarted. The Thomas write rule is a saving: an obsolete write is ignored instead of causing a restart. Validation based control is optimistic, because transactions run freely and are checked only at commit, in the read, validation and write phases. The gain over locking is that neither method makes a transaction wait, so no deadlock can form.
card.example: Two transactions start together and the one with the smaller timestamp is treated as older. If a younger transaction has already overwritten the item, the older transaction's late write is ignored rather than forced to restart.

quiz.q: What happens to a transaction whose operation arrives after a younger one has already used the item?
options: It waits for the younger one to finish
It is restarted with a new timestamp
quiz.why: Timestamp ordering never waits; the late transaction is rolled back and started again.

quiz.q: What does the Thomas write rule do?
options: Forces all writes to wait for a lock
Converts a shared lock into an exclusive lock
Ignores an obsolete write instead of restarting the transaction
quiz.why: If a younger transaction has already overwritten the value, the older write is obsolete and can be skipped.

quiz.q: Which statement about concurrency methods is NOT correct?
options: Timestamp ordering can cause restarts but not deadlock
Validation methods check for conflicts at commit time
Optimistic control has read, validation and write phases
Locking methods are free of deadlock because they never wait
quiz.why: Locking is the method that waits for locks, and that waiting is exactly what allows a deadlock to form.

quiz.q: What are the three phases of validation based concurrency control?
quiz.why: The transaction reads freely, is validated against the others at commit, then writes if it passes.

quiz.q: Which method never makes a transaction wait for another?
quiz.why: Timestamp and validation methods refuse and restart instead of blocking, so no waiting cycle appears.

card.examTip: Compare locking, timestamp ordering and validation in one table with the columns waiting, deadlock, restarts and when the check happens.

topics.title: Granularity of Data Items
topics.definition: Granularity refers to the size of the unit locked, from a single field up to the whole database.

children.title: Trade-off of granularity
children.definition: Small items allow more concurrency but more lock overhead, while large items do the opposite.

children.title: Multiple granularity locking
children.definition: Locks are taken at several levels of the hierarchy with intention locks.

children.title: Intention shared and intention exclusive locks
children.definition: IS and IX locks on ancestors signal that a descendant will be locked in shared or exclusive mode.

children.title: Compatibility of intention locks
children.definition: The compatibility matrix decides which combinations may be granted at the same time.

card.explanation: Granularity is how big the piece is that a lock covers. A small unit such as one row lets many transactions work at once, but the system must track a great many locks. A large unit such as a whole table is cheap to track and blocks almost everything, so concurrency suffers. Multiple granularity locking lets a transaction lock at the level it needs, using a hierarchy from database down to record. Intention locks mark the ancestors of the item being locked: IS means a descendant will be read, IX means one will be written. A compatibility matrix then decides which combinations may be granted together.
card.example: Updating one row out of ten thousand should lock that row, not the table. Reading a whole report may lock the table once, which is cheaper than ten thousand row locks.

quiz.q: What does a coarse granularity give?
options: High concurrency and high lock overhead
Low lock overhead and low concurrency
quiz.why: One big lock is cheap to track, but it blocks transactions that only wanted a different part of the data.

quiz.q: What does an intention shared (IS) lock signal?
options: The whole database is locked exclusively
The lock has been released already
The item itself is locked for writing
A descendant of this item will be locked in shared mode
quiz.why: Intention locks are taken on ancestors to announce what is going to be locked below them.

quiz.q: Which statement about granularity is NOT correct?
options: The database level is the finest granularity available
Fine granularity increases the number of locks to track
Intention locks are taken on the ancestors of an item
quiz.why: The whole database is the coarsest unit; a single field or one record is the finest.

quiz.q: A transaction wants to update a few rows deep inside one table. Which choice is best?
options: Lock the whole database for reading
Take an IX lock on the table and X locks on the rows
Take a shared lock on the whole table
Take no locks and rely on timestamps
quiz.why: The intention exclusive lock on the table announces the writes, and the row locks keep the rest available.

card.examTip: Draw the hierarchy database, table, page, record as a tree, and write IS, IX, S and X at the levels involved.

topics.title: Recovery Concepts
topics.definition: Recovery restores the database to a consistent state after a failure and ensures committed work is not lost.

children.title: Types of failure
children.definition: Transaction failure, system crash, media failure and natural disasters need different recovery responses.

children.title: Storage structure and stable storage
children.definition: Volatile memory, non volatile disk and stable storage mirrored across sites define what survives a crash.

children.title: Log based recovery
children.definition: A log records before images, after images and transaction events; deferred and immediate update policies use it differently.

children.title: Checkpoints
children.definition: Periodically flush the log and buffers so that recovery need not scan the whole log.

children.title: Shadow paging
children.definition: Maintains a current and a shadow page table, switching atomically on commit, which avoids a log but fragments storage.

children.title: ARIES recovery algorithm
children.definition: Uses write ahead logging, repeating history and fuzzy checkpoints in analysis, redo and undo passes.

card.explanation: Recovery brings the database back to a consistent state after something goes wrong. Failures fall into four kinds: the transaction itself fails, the system crashes, the media is lost, or the site is destroyed. The log is the main tool, because it records before images, after images and the events of each transaction. With it, undo rolls back a transaction that never committed and redo repeats one that did. Checkpoints shorten recovery, because work before the checkpoint is already known to be safe. ARIES is the common algorithm, using write ahead logging, repeating history and fuzzy checkpoints in three passes: analysis, redo and undo.
card.example: A power cut during a fee payment leaves some rows half updated. The log tells recovery which transactions had committed, so their writes are repeated and the others are undone.

quiz.q: Which pass of ARIES repeats the writes of committed transactions?
quiz.why: Redo repeats history so that every committed write is on disk, whatever happened before the crash.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a checkpoint?
options: To convert shared locks to exclusive locks
To shorten recovery by flushing the log and buffers
quiz.why: Everything before the checkpoint is already safe, so recovery starts from there instead of from the beginning.

quiz.q: Which statement about recovery is NOT correct?
options: A media failure is handled in the same way as a transaction failure
Stable storage is meant to survive any single failure
Shadow paging avoids a log but fragments storage
Write ahead logging puts the log record on disk before the data page
quiz.why: Media loss needs the last backup plus the archived log, while a transaction failure only needs undo.

quiz.q: Which technique keeps a current and a shadow page table and switches between them on commit?
quiz.why: Shadow paging makes commit atomic by switching page tables, at the cost of scattered pages on disk.

quiz.q: In deferred update, when are changes written to the database?
options: Only when the buffer is full
Immediately, before the log record is written
quiz.why: Deferred update keeps changes in the log until commit, so an aborted transaction needs no undo at all.

card.examTip: Name the four failure types, then say what each needs: undo, redo, or the backup plus archived log.

topics.title: Database Security Issues
topics.definition: Database security protects data from unauthorised access, disclosure and modification.

children.title: Access control and authorisation
children.definition: Discretionary and mandatory access control models grant privileges to users and roles.

children.title: Views and query modification
children.definition: Restricting a user to a view exposes only the rows and columns they may see.

children.title: Encryption and auditing
children.definition: Data is encrypted in storage or transit, and audit trails record who did what.

children.title: Statistical database security
children.definition: Statistical queries must not allow inference of individual values; techniques include query restriction, perturbation and auditing.

card.explanation: Database security keeps data away from people who should not read or change it. Discretionary access control lets the owner of an object grant privileges to others, while mandatory access control assigns security levels and compares them. A view is a simple tool: give a user only the view, and they see only the rows and columns it holds. Encryption protects data in storage and while it travels across a network, and an audit trail records who did what and when. Statistical databases need their own care, because averages and counts can be combined to reveal one person's value.
card.example: A clerk is given a view showing only customer names and cities, never the account balances. Running one query on five people and another on four can reveal the fifth person's salary, which is the inference problem.

quiz.q: Which control model lets the owner of a table grant privileges to other users?
quiz.why: Discretionary control is based on the owner's decision to grant or revoke a privilege.

quiz.q: How does a view improve security?
options: It exposes only the rows and columns the view contains
It makes the table read faster
It removes the need for an audit trail
quiz.why: The user queries the view and never reaches the columns that were left out of it.

quiz.q: Which statement about database security is NOT correct?
options: Statistical queries can leak an individual value by inference
Mandatory access control lets any owner grant away their privileges
An audit trail records who accessed what and when
Encryption protects data in storage and in transit
quiz.why: Granting privileges at the owner's discretion is discretionary control; mandatory control compares fixed security levels.

quiz.q: A user counts all employees, then counts all but one, and works out the missing salary. What is this called?
options: An inference attack on a statistical database
quiz.why: Query restriction, perturbation and output auditing are the usual defences against this kind of leak.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a usual defence for statistical database security?
options: Auditing the queries that were answered
Granting every user full read access
quiz.why: The three defences limit what may be asked, add noise to the answer, or watch what has been released.

card.examTip: Write the four headings access control, views, encryption and auditing, then add the inference problem with its three defences.

topics.title: File Organisation and Operations
topics.definition: A file is stored as records in blocks on disk, and its organisation decides how efficiently records are found and updated.

children.title: File operations
children.definition: Insertion, deletion, modification and retrieval of records identified by a search key.

children.title: Heap file organisation
children.definition: Records are placed wherever space is free, which makes insertion fast but search slow.

children.title: Sequential file organisation
children.definition: Records are kept in order of a search key, so search and ordered retrieval are fast while insertion needs reorganisation.

children.title: Hashing and indexed organisation
children.definition: A hash function or index computes the location directly, trading space and maintenance for speed.

children.title: Blocking factor and record layout
children.definition: Fixed or variable length records are packed into blocks, and the blocking factor is the records per block.

card.explanation: A file is a collection of records held in blocks on disk, and the organisation decides what is fast and what is slow. The four operations are insertion, deletion, modification and retrieval of a record found by its search key. In a heap file records go wherever there is free space, so insertion is quick and search is slow. A sequential file keeps the records ordered by the search key, so search and ordered listing are fast while insertion needs the file rearranged. Hashing and indexing compute the location instead, trading extra space and maintenance for speed.
card.example: Mark sheets pinned into a folder in the order they arrive make a heap file. Sorted by roll number they become a sequential file, and finding one student becomes quick.

quiz.q: Which file organisation gives fast insertion but slow search?
quiz.why: A heap file places each new record wherever there is room, so there is no order to search on.

quiz.q: What is the blocking factor?
options: The time taken to read one record
The number of records that fit in one block
The number of blocks in the file
The size of the search key
quiz.why: Blocking factor is records per block, and it decides how many disk accesses a full scan needs.

quiz.q: Which statement about file organisation is NOT correct?
options: Sequential files keep records ordered by the search key
Hashed files find a record by computing its address
Sequential files make insertion cheap because no order is kept
Heap files keep no order among the records
quiz.why: Keeping the order is what makes insertion expensive in a sequential file, since records must be moved.

quiz.q: A file holds 10,000 records of 100 bytes each in blocks of 1,000 bytes. What is the blocking factor?
quiz.why: Blocking factor is the block size divided by the record size, so 1,000 divided by 100 gives 10.

quiz.q: Which key is used to identify the record being searched for?
quiz.why: Any field used to locate a record is a search key, whether or not its values are unique.

card.examTip: List the four operations, then give one line each on heap, sequential, hashed and indexed with what is fast and what is slow.

topics.title: Hashing Techniques
topics.definition: Hashing applies a function to the search key to compute the bucket where the record is stored.

children.title: Static hashing
children.definition: A fixed number of buckets is chosen in advance; the file grows slowly and long overflow chains appear.

children.title: Collision and overflow handling
children.definition: Open addressing, chaining within a bucket and multiple hashing resolve records that map to a full bucket.

children.title: Dynamic and extendible hashing
children.definition: The number of buckets grows and shrinks with the data by splitting buckets and using a directory of pointer bits.

children.title: Comparison of hashing with indexing
children.definition: Hashing is excellent for equality searches but useless for range queries, where indexes are preferred.

card.explanation: Hashing runs the search key through a function and uses the answer as a bucket address. In static hashing the number of buckets is fixed in advance, so a growing file develops long overflow chains. A collision is when a record lands in a bucket that is already full, handled by open addressing, chaining or a second hash function. Extendible hashing lets the directory grow and shrink, splitting one bucket at a time as the file grows. Hashing is excellent for finding one exact record, but it cannot answer a range query at all, which is where an index wins.
card.example: A library hashes the book accession number to a shelf number, so one book is found directly. Asking for every book added last month cannot use the hash, because the buckets hold books in no useful order.

quiz.q: What happens in static hashing as the file keeps growing?
options: The records are sorted inside each bucket
quiz.why: The bucket count is fixed, so extra records pile into overflow and searches slow down.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a way of handling a collision?
quiz.why: Open addressing, chaining and a second hash function resolve collisions; sorting does not.

quiz.q: Why is hashing unsuitable for a range query?
options: Hash tables cannot hold many records
The directory would grow too large
The hash function is too slow
Buckets hold records in no order that matches the key
quiz.why: The hash scatters keys across buckets, so nearby keys are not stored near each other.

quiz.q: What does extendible hashing do when a bucket overflows?
options: It splits that bucket and grows the directory
It moves the record to overflow and leaves it there
It switches over to a B+ tree
It rebuilds the whole table with more buckets
quiz.why: Only the overflowing bucket is split, and the directory uses one more bit for that part.

quiz.q: Which operation is hashing best at?
options: Finding every record in a key range
Finding one record with a known exact key
Listing the records in sorted order
Finding the smallest key in the file
quiz.why: An exact match goes straight to one bucket, which is usually a single disk access.

card.examTip: Draw a bucket directory with two bits of the hash, then show one split. Finish with the line that hashing cannot do range queries.

topics.title: Indexing and Types of Indexes
topics.definition: An index is an auxiliary file of key and pointer pairs that speeds up retrieval from the main file.

children.title: Primary index
children.definition: Built on the ordered key field of a sequentially ordered file, with one entry per block.

children.title: Clustering index
children.definition: Defined on an ordered non key field, so several records can share the same index value.

children.title: Secondary index
children.definition: Built on a non ordered field, giving one entry per distinct value with pointers to blocks.

children.title: Dense and sparse indexes
children.definition: A dense index has an entry for every search key value while a sparse index has entries for some values only.

children.title: Single level and multilevel indexes
children.definition: When the index itself becomes large it is indexed again, forming a multilevel structure like an ISAM tree.

children.title: Indexes on multiple keys
children.definition: Composite indexes order by the concatenation of keys, and grid or partitioned hashing handles multiattribute equality queries.

card.explanation: An index is a small auxiliary file holding key and pointer pairs, so a record can be found without scanning the whole data file. A primary index is built on the ordering key field of a sequential file and holds one entry per block. A clustering index is built on an ordering field that is not a key, so several records may share one index entry. A secondary index is built on a field with no order at all, and it needs one entry per distinct value. A dense index has an entry for every search key value, while a sparse index has entries for only some of them. When an index itself grows too large to scan, it is indexed again, which gives a multilevel structure such as an ISAM tree.
card.example: The index at the back of a book is a secondary index. It maps each term to page numbers, and the pages themselves are not ordered by that term.

quiz.q: Which index is built on the ordering key field of a sequential file?
quiz.why: A primary index follows the ordering key of the file and holds one entry for each block.

quiz.q: How does a dense index differ from a sparse index?
options: A dense index is stored on disk and a sparse one in memory
A sparse index holds more entries than a dense one
A dense index can only be built on a primary key
A dense index has an entry for every search key value
quiz.why: A sparse index saves space by holding entries for only some key values, one per block.

quiz.q: Which statement about indexes is NOT correct?
options: A primary index can only be built on an unordered file
A multilevel index puts an index on the index
A clustering index is built on an ordering non key field
A secondary index needs one entry per distinct value
quiz.why: A primary index needs the file to be ordered on that key; an unordered file needs a secondary index.

quiz.q: An index has grown so large that scanning it is slow. What is the usual answer?
options: Build an index on the index
Convert the file into a hash file
Split the data file into two
quiz.why: Indexing the index gives a multilevel structure, which is how ISAM and tree indexes work.

quiz.q: Which index suits a field where many records share the same value and the file is ordered on it?
quiz.why: A clustering index is built on an ordering field that is not unique, so one entry points at a cluster.

card.examTip: Give one line each on primary, clustering and secondary, then add dense versus sparse. Sketch the multilevel index if the question carries marks for a diagram.

topics.title: B Tree and B+ Tree
topics.definition: B trees and B+ trees are balanced multilevel search structures designed for disk storage with a high branching factor.

children.title: B tree properties
children.definition: All leaves are at the same level, nodes hold between a minimum and maximum number of keys, and a node with k keys has k + 1 children.

children.title: B+ tree properties
children.definition: Internal nodes hold only keys and pointers while all data pointers live in a linked list of leaves.

children.title: Insertion in a B+ tree
children.definition: Insert into the correct leaf and split it when full, pushing the middle key into the parent and possibly splitting upwards to the root.

children.title: Deletion in a B+ tree
children.definition: Remove the entry, redistribute keys with a sibling or merge nodes when a node falls below the minimum occupancy.
