children.title: B tree versus B+ tree
children.definition: B trees store data pointers in internal nodes and B+ trees do not, so B+ trees have higher fan-out and faster range scans.

children.title: Why B+ trees dominate databases
children.definition: A high fan-out keeps the tree shallow, so a record is found in three or four disk accesses even for millions of records.

card.explanation: A B tree is a balanced search tree built for disk, where every leaf sits at the same level. Each node holds many keys, and one node is sized to fill a disk block. One read then brings in a whole set of comparisons. A node with k keys has k plus one children, and every node except the root must be at least half full. A B+ tree keeps data pointers only in the leaves and joins those leaves in a linked list. That makes the fan-out higher and the range scan a straight walk along the list, which is why databases use B+ trees.
card.example: With a fan-out of 100, a B+ tree of three levels already holds a million keys. Finding one record then costs three disk reads instead of scanning a million rows.

quiz.q: Where does a B+ tree keep the pointers to the actual records?
options: In both the internal nodes and the leaves
quiz.why: Internal nodes hold only keys and pointers to lower nodes, so all data pointers sit in the linked leaves.

quiz.q: A node in a B tree holds k keys. How many children does it have?
quiz.why: Keys separate the children, so k keys split the node into k plus one subtrees.

quiz.q: Which statement about B+ trees is NOT correct?
options: Every node except the root is at least half full
A B+ tree stores record pointers in its internal nodes
All the leaves are at the same level
The leaves are linked for fast range scans
quiz.why: Keeping internal nodes free of data pointers is what raises the fan-out and keeps the tree shallow.

quiz.q: A leaf is full and a new key must go into it. What happens?
options: The key is placed in an overflow area
The leaf is split and the middle key moves up
quiz.why: Splitting can cascade upwards, and splitting the root is how the tree gains a level.

quiz.q: What happens when a deletion leaves a node below the minimum occupancy?
options: The key is put back where it was
The tree switches to a hash file
The tree is rebuilt from scratch
Keys are shared with a sibling, or the nodes are merged
quiz.why: Redistribution is tried first, and merging two nodes is the fallback when a sibling cannot spare a key.

card.examTip: Sketch a B+ tree with linked leaves, then note the two reasons it wins: higher fan-out and a straight walk along the leaves.

topics.title: Object Oriented Database Management Systems
topics.definition: An OODBMS stores objects with their methods and supports the object oriented features of programming languages directly.

children.title: Need for OODBMS
children.definition: Applications with complex data such as CAD, multimedia and GIS suffer from the impedance mismatch between objects and tables.

children.title: Features
children.definition: Object identity, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and persistence are supported natively.

children.title: Object oriented data model
children.definition: Objects have identity and state, classes define types, and relationships are captured through references and collections.

children.title: Object oriented languages and persistence
children.definition: Languages such as C++ and Java are extended with a persistent object store, or pure OO languages such as Smalltalk are used.

children.title: Advantages and disadvantages
children.definition: Excellent for complex data and navigational access, but weak for ad hoc queries and lacking a common standard.

card.explanation: An object oriented database stores objects, with their state and their methods, instead of rows in tables. It exists because applications such as computer aided design, multimedia and geographic systems hold data too complex to flatten. The mismatch between program objects and table rows is called the impedance mismatch, and an OODBMS removes it. Object identity, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and persistence are all supported directly by the database. The cost is weaker support for ad hoc queries and the absence of one common standard, which kept these systems out of the mainstream.
card.example: A circuit design holds thousands of connected parts, each with its own behaviour. Storing it as objects keeps the connections and the code together, while flattening it into tables would need dozens of joined tables.

quiz.q: What is the impedance mismatch?
options: The gap between program objects and table rows
A fault in the network cable
The extra cost of a licence
quiz.why: Objects carry identity, nesting and methods, which do not map cleanly onto flat rows and columns.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a feature of an object oriented database?
options: One query standard agreed by every vendor
quiz.why: The features are native, but the lack of a common standard is the main weakness of these systems.

quiz.q: Which application area pushed the need for object oriented databases?
options: Computer aided design and geographic systems
quiz.why: Complex, deeply connected data is hard to flatten into tables, which is where these systems help.

quiz.q: Which statement about an OODBMS is NOT correct?
options: It stores objects together with their methods
It suits navigational access through references
It is weaker than a relational system for ad hoc queries
It replaced the relational model in most commercial products
quiz.why: Relational systems stayed dominant, and object relational features were added to them instead.

card.examTip: Define OODBMS, give the impedance mismatch as the reason, list five features, then write two advantages and two disadvantages.

topics.title: Object Relational Databases
topics.definition: An object relational DBMS extends the relational model with objects, inheritance, complex types and methods.

children.title: Object relational features
children.definition: User defined types, collections such as arrays and nested tables, references and object identifiers.

children.title: Bridging objects and tables
children.definition: Object relational mapping persists programming objects as rows and columns.

children.title: Comparison of the three approaches
children.definition: RDBMS flatten complex data, OODBMS lose SQL simplicity and ORDBMS keep both, which is why commercial systems follow this route.

card.explanation: An object relational system keeps the relational model and adds object features to it. Tables can use user defined types, hold collections such as arrays and nested tables, and carry references and object identifiers. Methods can be attached to a type, so a value knows what it can do. This lets a program's objects be stored as rows without throwing away SQL, which is what object relational mapping does. It is the middle way: relational systems flatten complex data, object oriented systems lose SQL, and object relational systems keep both.
card.example: An address can be one user defined type holding street, city and pin code. It sits in a customer row as one column, and reports still run plain SQL.

quiz.q: What does an object relational DBMS add to the relational model?
options: User defined types, collections, references and methods
A hash based storage engine only
Nothing, it is only a new name
quiz.why: These additions let complex values sit inside a row while SQL still works on the table.

quiz.q: What is object relational mapping?
options: Drawing an ER diagram for an object model
Persisting program objects as rows and columns
Converting a table into a hash file
Splitting a table into two for normalisation
quiz.why: The mapping layer moves data between the objects a program uses and the rows a database stores.

quiz.q: Which statement about the three approaches is NOT correct?
options: Object oriented systems give up the simplicity of SQL
Object relational systems keep tables and add object features
Object relational systems cannot run SQL at all
Relational systems flatten complex data into tables
quiz.why: Keeping SQL is the whole point of the object relational route, which is why vendors followed it.

quiz.q: Which kind of value can be stored as one column in an object relational table?
options: A nested table or an array
quiz.why: Collections such as arrays and nested tables are part of what the object relational model added.

card.examTip: Compare RDBMS, OODBMS and ORDBMS in one table with the columns storage unit, query language, complex data and typical use.

topics.title: XML and Semi-structured Data
topics.definition: XML is a text based, self describing format for exchanging hierarchical data between systems.

children.title: Structure of XML
children.definition: A prolog, nested elements with tags, attributes, entities and text content form a well formed document.

children.title: DTD and XML Schema
children.definition: Define the allowed elements, attributes and structure, so documents can be validated.

children.title: Parsing and querying XML
children.definition: DOM and SAX parsers read documents and XPath, XQuery and XSLT select and transform the data.

children.title: Storing XML in a database
children.definition: Documents may be stored as CLOB values, shredded into tables or kept in native XML columns.

card.explanation: XML is a text format where the tags travel with the data, so a document describes itself. A well formed document has a prolog, one root element and properly nested elements with attributes and text. A DTD or an XML Schema says which elements and attributes are allowed, so a document can be checked before it is used. Programs read a document with a DOM parser, which builds a tree in memory, or a SAX parser, which reports events as it reads. XPath and XQuery select parts of a document, and XSLT transforms it. A database may store the document whole, shred it into tables or keep it in a native XML column.
card.example: A college sends a student list to the university as XML, with one element per student and an attribute for the roll number. The receiving system reads it even though it runs different software.

quiz.q: Which part of an XML document declares which elements and attributes are allowed?
options: A DTD or an XML Schema
quiz.why: A DTD or a schema is the grammar of the document, and it is what validation is checked against.

quiz.q: Which parser builds a full tree of the document in memory?
quiz.why: DOM holds the whole tree so any node can be revisited; SAX reports events once and keeps nothing.

quiz.q: Which statement about storing XML is NOT correct?
options: A document can be shredded into relational tables
A document can be kept in a native XML column
A document must be shredded, because no other option exists
A document can be stored whole as a large character object
quiz.why: All three storage choices exist, and the right one depends on how the data will be queried.

quiz.q: Which language is used to select nodes from an XML document?
quiz.why: XPath addresses nodes by path and condition; XQuery extends it and XSLT transforms the result.

quiz.q: What makes XML self describing?
options: The tags travel with the data
Only one program can read it
It needs a schema before it can be read
It is stored in binary form
quiz.why: The element names sit inside the file, so a reader understands the structure without outside help.

card.examTip: Show a four line XML sample, then name the DTD or schema for validation, the two parsers, and the query languages.

topics.title: Temporal Databases
topics.definition: Temporal databases record time so that past, present and future states of the data can be queried.

children.title: Valid time and transaction time
children.definition: Valid time is when a fact is true in the real world; transaction time is when it was stored in the database.

children.title: Bitemporal databases
children.definition: Track both kinds of time, allowing corrections and audit of what the system believed at any moment.

children.title: Temporal operators
children.definition: Queries use operators such as overlaps, contains, precedes and during on time intervals.

children.title: Applications
children.definition: Banking audit trails, medical records, insurance history and employee service records.

card.explanation: A conventional database keeps only the current value, so an old value is lost the moment it is overwritten. A temporal database keeps time with the data and answers questions about the past. Valid time is when a fact was true in the real world, and transaction time is when the database recorded it. A bitemporal database keeps both, so it can say what was true on a date and what the system believed at the time. Queries then use interval operators such as overlaps, contains, precedes and during. Typical uses are banking audit trails, medical records, insurance history and employee service records.
card.example: A salary changed in April but the record was corrected in June. Valid time says April and transaction time says June, so the database can show both what was true and when it was learned.

quiz.q: What is valid time?
options: When the database stored the record
When the fact was true in the real world
quiz.why: Valid time is about the real world; transaction time is about when the system recorded it.

quiz.q: What does a bitemporal database keep?
options: Both valid time and transaction time
quiz.why: Keeping both lets a query ask what was true and what the system knew, as two separate questions.

quiz.q: Which statement about temporal databases is NOT correct?
options: They answer questions about past states of the data
Banking audit trails are a typical use
Interval operators include overlaps and during
They store only the latest value of every fact
quiz.why: Storing only the latest value is what a conventional database does; a temporal one keeps the history.

quiz.q: Which operator tests whether two time intervals share any period?
quiz.why: Overlaps is true when the two intervals have at least one instant in common.

quiz.q: A correction is made in June to a salary that changed in April. Which times differ?
options: Valid time is April, transaction time is June
Valid time is June, transaction time is April
quiz.why: The real world change and the moment the system learned of it are two separate facts.

card.examTip: Define valid time and transaction time with one example each, then say that a bitemporal database keeps both and give two applications.

topics.title: Mobile Databases
topics.definition: A mobile database runs on portable devices and synchronises with a central database over wireless links.

children.title: Challenges
children.definition: Frequent disconnection, limited bandwidth, low battery and small memory change the design assumptions.

children.title: Data synchronisation and replication
children.definition: Changes made offline are reconciled later, which can raise conflicts that need resolution rules.

children.title: Mobile transactions
children.definition: Long lived, location dependent transactions require relaxed ACID properties in some systems.

card.explanation: A mobile database lives on a portable device and syncs with a central server over a wireless link. The assumptions of a fixed network no longer hold. The device is often disconnected, the bandwidth is limited, the battery is small and the memory is tight. Changes are therefore made on the device and reconciled with the server later, which is what synchronisation and replication do. That reconciliation can produce conflicts, so rules are needed to decide which change wins. Mobile transactions are long lived and location dependent, and some systems relax the ACID rules to let them finish.
card.example: A sales representative records orders on a tablet with no signal. At the office the orders are reconciled with the central database, and a rule settles any clash with a newer price.

quiz.q: Which is NOT listed as a challenge for mobile databases?
options: Too many indexes on the server
quiz.why: The challenges come from the device and the link: disconnection, bandwidth, battery and memory.

quiz.q: What happens when a device reconnects after working offline?
options: The server is rebuilt from the device
Nothing, because the two stay separate
Its changes are reconciled with the central database
quiz.why: Synchronisation compares the two copies, applies the differences and resolves conflicts as it goes.

quiz.q: Why are mobile transactions described as long lived?
options: They may stay open across disconnections and movement between cells
They always take more than an hour
quiz.why: A transaction can span a journey and several network cells, so it runs far longer than a desktop one.

quiz.q: Which statement about mobile databases is NOT correct?
options: Replication keeps a copy of the data on the device
A mobile database needs a constant wired connection to work
Conflicts need resolution rules during synchronisation
Some systems relax the ACID properties for mobile work
quiz.why: Working while disconnected is the whole point, and it is what makes synchronisation necessary.

card.examTip: List the four challenges, then explain synchronisation and conflict resolution, then add why ACID is sometimes relaxed.

topics.title: Spatial Databases
topics.definition: Spatial databases store geometric objects such as points, lines and polygons and answer location based queries.

children.title: Spatial data types and queries
children.definition: Point, line and region types support queries like "find all hospitals within 5 km".

children.title: Spatial indexing
children.definition: R trees, quad trees and grid files organise two dimensional data for fast region queries.

children.title: Applications
children.definition: Geographic information systems, maps, navigation, urban planning and location based services.

card.explanation: A spatial database stores geometric objects and answers questions about where things are. The basic types are point, line and region, and the queries ask things like finding every hospital within five kilometres. Ordinary indexes do not help, because they order values along one dimension while spatial data covers two. Spatial indexes such as R trees, quad trees and grid files organise the data by area. A region query then visits only the blocks it overlaps. Typical uses are geographic information systems, maps, navigation, urban planning and location based services.
card.example: A delivery app asks for every driver within three kilometres of a pickup point. An R tree groups nearby drivers into rectangles, so the search reads only a few blocks instead of every row.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a basic spatial data type?
quiz.why: Point, line and region are the geometric types; integer is a plain relational type.

quiz.q: Why does a normal B+ tree index work poorly for spatial data?
options: It is too slow to build
It cannot be stored on disk
It orders values along one dimension only
quiz.why: Spatial data covers two dimensions, so an index that sorts along one axis loses the neighbour information.

quiz.q: Which index organises spatial objects by grouping nearby ones into rectangles?
quiz.why: An R tree groups objects by their bounding rectangles, which suits area and nearest neighbour queries.

quiz.q: Which statement about spatial databases is NOT correct?
options: Quad trees and grid files are spatial indexes
They store only text descriptions of places
Navigation apps are a typical use
quiz.why: They store real geometry, which is what makes distance and containment queries possible.

quiz.q: Which application is least likely to need a spatial database?
options: A flood risk model for a district
A payroll system for office staff
quiz.why: Payroll has no geometry in it, so a plain relational design is enough.

card.examTip: Name the three spatial types, one example query, three index structures and three applications.

topics.title: Case Study: Designing and Managing a Project Database
topics.definition: A case study ties the whole module together by taking one application from requirements to a working, normalised database.

children.title: Requirement analysis
children.definition: Identify entities, attributes, relationships, constraints and reports the users need.

children.title: Conceptual and logical design
children.definition: Draw the ER diagram, map it to relations, choose keys and normalise up to 3NF or BCNF.

children.title: Physical design and implementation
children.definition: Choose file organisation, indexes, constraints, views, triggers and the required privileges.

children.title: Maintenance and tuning
children.definition: Monitor performance, rebuild indexes, back up regularly and handle schema evolution.

card.explanation: A case study runs one application through every stage the syllabus has covered. Requirement analysis lists the entities, attributes, relationships, constraints and the reports the users expect. Conceptual design turns that list into an ER diagram. Logical design maps the diagram into relations, picks the keys and normalises up to 3NF or BCNF. Physical design chooses the file organisation, the indexes, the constraints, the views, the triggers and the privileges each role needs. After release the work continues: watch the performance, rebuild the indexes, back up on a schedule and manage changes to the schema.
card.example: A college library project starts from the list of books, members and loans. It ends with normalised tables, an index on the accession number, a view for the student portal and a weekly backup.

quiz.q: What is produced during conceptual design?
options: The file organisation and the indexes
An ER diagram of entities and relationships
quiz.why: Conceptual design is the diagram; physical design is what chooses indexes, files and privileges.

quiz.q: At which stage are the tables normalised up to 3NF or BCNF?
quiz.why: Logical design maps the ER diagram into relations, chooses the keys and removes the anomalies.

quiz.q: Which statement about the stages is NOT correct?
options: Maintenance includes rebuilding indexes and backing up
Conceptual design decides the storage layout on disk
Requirement analysis lists the entities and the reports needed
Physical design chooses indexes and file organisation
quiz.why: Storage layout belongs to physical design; conceptual design is still a diagram of entities.

quiz.q: Which of these belongs to maintenance rather than to initial implementation?
options: Rebuilding an index after heavy updates
Deciding the privileges of a role
quiz.why: Rebuilding indexes and monitoring performance are ongoing jobs that start after release.

quiz.q: What is the usual order of the stages in a database project?
quiz.why: Each stage feeds the next: what is needed, what it looks like, how it is stored, how it is tuned.

card.examTip: Write the four stages as headings and put two bullet points under each. Case study marks usually come from showing the order.
